## A Framework for Democratic Resilience

Democratic resilience is not a stock of features but a functioning feedback loop [@easton1965]: demands and support convert into outputs, fed back into the next round of inputs. Input carries citizen demands and external shocks. Throughput is the political system. Output is policy. Feedback returns information to citizens and institutions.

Throughput cycles through six functions — participation, aggregation, communication, policymaking, power, adjudication — each carried by its own institutions (elections and civil society, parties and media, legislature and bureaucracy, executive, judiciary). Communication and adjudication extend the classical structural-functional account: information flow, and the check on the others, cannot be left out.

At the loop's centre sits one contest: who holds authority over information. Open, accountable authority reinforces resilience. Closed, captured authority erodes it (Figure 1).

**Open questions**: How to better connect informationalism with democratic resilience. Literature to support the open/public good vs closed/captured info claim. Are the identified functions really the core components or are we missing some?

## How AI Enters the Loop

Before generative AI, the tools that fought over authority over information — the internet, algorithms, platforms — stayed neutral in how they interpreted what they carried. Generative AI does not: it acts on information, not just carries it.

This crystallises into epistemic offloading: ceding sovereignty over information to generative AI. Generative AI is inert until tasked, but its output is commonly accepted without independent verification. Its sheer volume is part of the reason: thorough verification is close to impossible for output at this scale, though how close depends on the task and the domain. That acceptance, not the tasking, is what transfers authority over information to the system, repeated at every stage of the loop. This is AI-mediated informationalism.

The effect is not symmetric. Closed, captured authority becomes diluted authority once generative AI mediates it unchecked: content controlled by whoever tasks the model without checking it, and information stops functioning as a public good [@garbemaerz2025; @maerz2026techautokratie]. Correction is possible — the same capability that dilutes can clarify [@noveck2021] — but only by design and validation, not by default (Figure 2).

**Open questions**: Do we only cover generative AI? Is our theory only valid for generative AI? Does anyone in the team cover other forms of AI? And the above needs much more support from the literature...epistemic offloading might also be to jargony.

::: {.content-visible unless-format="docx"}
```{=latex}
\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.75\linewidth]{figures/fig_epistemic_offloading.pdf}
\caption{Epistemic offloading, drawn on Figure 1's balance: sovereignty over information passes to generative AI the moment its output goes unchecked, tilting the contest toward dilution by default. Correction takes deliberate design and validation to tip it back.}
\label{fig:offloading}
\end{figure}
```

## Work Packages

Each work package below asks one question of one part of the loop: how does AI-mediated informationalism reshape it?
